note: Josephus names 'John, that was called the Baptist', a good man who commanded the Jews to exercise virtue and come to baptism, and records Herod Antipas putting him to death.
Josephus confirms John the Baptist as a real preacher who drew crowds and was executed by Herod; he never mentions the wilderness of Judea, so the verse's location stays unconfirmed.

Josephus says John 'commanded the Jews to exercise virtue, both as to righteousness towards one another, and piety towards God' - a preacher of repentance, though he says nothing of the Kingdom of Heaven.
'Now when [many] others came in crowds about him, for they were very greatly moved [or pleased] by hearing his words' - mass crowds gathered to John, though Josephus names no originating regions.
Josephus confirms that John administered a washing with water to Jews who came to him; he does not state the place, so the Jordan setting rests on the gospel text.
Josephus attests John's fame and his crowds, the setting into which Matthew places Jesus' journey to the Jordan; he never mentions Jesus' baptism.
Josephus situates John's movement among the Jews under Herod Antipas and Aretas; the general Judean setting is contextual, not a naming of the wilderness of Judea.

Josephus: 'The Jews had for a great while had three sects of philosophy peculiar to themselves; the sect of the Essens, and the sect of the Sadducees, and the third sort of opinions was that of those called Pharisees' - both parties of Matt 3:7 named as real groups.

Wikipedia (John 1:23, citing Keener): 'the Qumran community applied Isaiah 40:3 to its own mission, using it to justify a total withdrawal into the wilderness (1QS 8:13-14)' - the same scriptural use Matthew makes, in John's environment.
1QS 8.13-14 shows a Jewish community of the period justifying total withdrawal into the wilderness by Isaiah 40:3 - the wilderness of Judea as a living religious setting.

Biblical cross-reference, not independent evidence: Wikipedia (Entomophagy in humans): 'for the ancient Israelites, Leviticus 11 prescribes allowing the consumption of four types of locusts' - locusts were permitted food in John's culture.

Biblical cross-reference, not independent evidence: Wikipedia (John the Baptist): 'Matthew and Mark describe John's attire in a way reminiscent of the description of Elijah in 2 Kings 1:8, who also wore a garment of hair and a leather belt' - the costume signals an Elijah-like prophet.

The Great Isaiah Scroll, dated ca. 125 BCE, contains the entire Book of Isaiah including chapter 40 - the prophecy Matthew quotes existed in Hebrew a century and a half before John. Graded B by architect decision: the scroll shows the quoted Isaiah text existed before Jesus, which is the specific point of a quotation claim.
The scroll was found in Qumran Cave 1 in the Judaean desert - the wilderness was a landscape of manuscripts and ascetic communities.

Al-Maghtas, a UNESCO site on the east bank of the Jordan, contains buildings 'with both aspects of a Jewish mikveh (ritual bath) resembling Second Temple period pools from Qumran', and has been venerated as John's baptism place since at least the Byzantine period.

The site is 'reputed to be the location of the Baptism of Jesus by John the Baptist and venerated as such since at least the Byzantine period'; its identification is disputed - the page quotes the Washington Post: 'There is no archaeological evidence of Jesus ever having been baptized in these waters', and Origen knew no Bethany east of the Jordan.
The site lies on the east bank of the Jordan River, fixing the river's course and its role as the baptism frontier between Judea and Perea.

At Qumran, 'Jewish ritual baths' were found among the excavated structures, and hundreds of Second Temple-period mikvot are known across the land - water-immersion was an established Jewish custom in John's region and period.
Wikipedia (Judaean Desert): 'The desert also attracted religious sects, including the classical-era Jewish ascetics of Qumran (likely Essenes)' - the wilderness was inhabited by ascetic communities.

The Al-Maghtas historicity section quotes the Washington Post: 'There is no archaeological evidence of Jesus ever having been baptized in these waters'; the identification rests on Byzantine-era veneration.
Origen, in the 3rd century, noticed 'there was no place called Bethany east of the Jordan' and suggested amending the name to Bethabara - the gospel place-name was already unstable.
Josephus's John baptises 'not in order to the putting away [or the remission] of some sins [only], but for the purification of the body' - unlike Matthew's 'baptism of repentance' for confessed sins.

Pliny (NH 5.73) locates the Esseni 'on the west of Asphaltites' (the Dead Sea), a settled ascetic Jewish community in the Judaean wilderness, 'marvellous beyond all others throughout the whole earth'.

Pliny does not mention John, but the Dead Sea wilderness he describes was home to the ascetic Esseni - contextual support for the wilderness of Judea as a living religious setting in the first century.

Al-Maghtas lies on the east bank of the Jordan, the 'beyond the Jordan' region that Matt 4:25 names as a source of the crowds; John's earlier activity at the Jordan ford (Matt 3) drew from the same region.
